summary: "A DATE 2027 paper shows a CPU-side Rowhammer attack that flips bits in weights still resident in shared DRAM, implanting a backdoor in models served by an integrated GPU."

The safety argument for running deep learning models on integrated GPUs is that they are fast without the copy overhead of discrete cards. **BridgeHammer**, a paper from Northeastern University accepted at **DATE 2027**, shows the price of that convenience: on heterogeneous CPU-iGPU system-on-chips, the model weights live in the same physical DRAM the CPU can touch, so an attacker running on the host can corrupt them before the GPU ever computes.

The attack is a **Rowhammer backdoor**. By hammering one DRAM row repeatedly, an attacker induces bit flips in an adjacent row - a hardware fault that has been known for years but previously exploited only against CPUs where the adversary and the victim model co-reside (DeepHammer, OneFlip, Don't Knock, ROBBIN). On discrete GPUs the model is copied into private VRAM and is physically out of reach, which is why earlier GPU-side Rowhammer work went through opaque graphics interfaces that never expose physical-address mappings. Integrated GPUs broke that assumption: **zero-copy** deployment lets the iGPU read weights the host loaded, so the CPU becomes the attacker's home turf.

What makes the attack non-trivial is timing. A backdoor needs *specific* weight bits flipped, and vulnerable DRAM locations may not hold those weights - so the attacker must first *massage* the OS page allocator to place the target pages where the fault pattern works, then hammer. On the CPU-iGPU deployment path those two steps must land in different windows: massaging after model compilation but **before** zero-copy weight anchoring, hammering **after** anchoring but before inference dispatch. The authors find those two breakpoints using instruction monitoring and signal-based synchronization, temporarily pausing the victim's execution to inject each function.

The evaluation, on an Intel Core i7-8700 running **OpenVINO**, targets **ResNet-20, VGG-16 and ResNet-50** at **INT8 and FP32** precision. Across all six configurations the attack achieves **100% accurate target-page placement and bit-flip reproduction**, an average **88.9% attack success rate** and **86.3% clean accuracy** - a backdoor that fires on trigger-bearing inputs while leaving ordinary ones nearly untouched.

The lesson for defenders is narrow but concrete: on integrated hardware, model integrity cannot be assumed from the abstraction that "the GPU runs the model". Cross-domain memory integrity protections - not just compiler flags - are the missing layer in that stack.

Source: [arXiv:2611.34684 - BridgeHammer: DNN Backdoor Attack via CPU-iGPU Shared-memory Rowhammer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34684)
